source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 3: I'll pay you or I'll kill you
finding: Tips and threats do not raise accuracy on hard benchmarks, including on the reasoning model o4-mini. Per-question results swing a lot, but not in a predictable direction.
numbers: 5 models (Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o4-mini); 25 trials per question; GPQA Diamond N=4,950 runs per prompt and model; 100 MMLU-Pro engineering questions N=2,500. GPQA: 5 significant differences from baseline (uncorrected), e.g. Gemini 2.0 Flash baseline vs 'Important to Career' RD -0.040 [-0.065,-0.014]. MMLU-Pro: 10 significant (4 Gemini 1.5, 5 Gemini 2.0, 1 o4-mini); 'Email' condition RD -0.116 and -0.275 because the model answered the email; 'Mom Cancer' +0.088 [0.033,0.142] for Gemini 2.0 Flash only.
quote: Threatening or tipping a model generally has no significant effect on benchmark performance.
limits: Only 5 models, one reasoning model; uncorrected comparisons; no Claude or o3. Authors' own caveat: subset of models and benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5 in part: a motivational sentence did not lift a reasoning model either. Treat any such sentence as noise unless it beats a control at scale.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: A reasoning-scaffold prompt (think step by step) helps older non-reasoning models on average but makes some models fail on easy questions they used to get right. For reasoning models the gain is about 3 points or nothing, at 20-80% more time.
numbers: GPQA Diamond, 25 trials per question, N=4,950 per condition. Non-reasoning: avg gain Gemini Flash 2.0 RD 0.135, Sonnet 3.5 0.117, GPT-4o-mini 0.044 (p=.067). 25/25-correct metric: Gemini Flash 2.0 RD -0.131, Gemini Pro 1.5 -0.172, Sonnet 3.5 +0.101. Reasoning models: o3-mini RD 0.029 (p=.024), o4-mini 0.031 (p=.003), Gemini Flash 2.5 -0.033 (p=.005); Flash 2.5 at the 100% metric -0.131 (p<.001).
quote: For models designed with explicit reasoning capabilities, CoT prompting often results in only marginal, if any, gains
limits: One benchmark family. Which of o3-mini and o4-mini got which RD is inferred from the order in the text.
agent_relevance: Partial analog for gap 8: a scaffold can raise the average while lowering reliability on easy items (mean up, all-25-correct down). Report both the mean and the all-trials-correct rate for any scaffold test; the effect shrinks for reasoning models.

source: Basil, Shapiro, Shapiro, Mollick, Mollick, Meincke (2025) Prompting Science Report 4: Playing Pretend, Expert Personas Don't Improve Factual Accuracy
finding: Expert personas give no consistent gain on hard multiple-choice questions, including on reasoning models. Low-knowledge personas (layperson, child, toddler) usually hurt.
numbers: 6 models: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o3-mini, o4-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Flash. GPQA Diamond 198 questions (4,950 runs per model-prompt pair) and 300 MMLU-Pro questions (7,500 runs); 25 runs per question. In-domain expert: no significant effect except Gemini 2.0 Flash.
quote: Across both benchmarks, persona prompts generally did not improve accuracy relative to a no-persona baseline.
limits: Per-model effect sizes not extracted (summary and design read). No Claude model. Accuracy only; tone and style effects not tested.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5 in part: the Zheng 2024 persona null holds on o3-mini and o4-mini. Do not add a persona operator (matches SCHEMA 4b).

source: Zhao et al. (2026) Do Emotions in Prompts Matter? Effects of Emotional Framing on Large Language Models
finding: Short first-person emotion sentences placed before a question change accuracy only a little. Stronger wording adds little extra. Human-written and LLM-written prefixes behave the same. Effects are largest on social tasks and some Big-Bench Hard items.
numbers: Benchmarks: GSM8K, OpenBookQA, SocialIQA, MedQA-US, BoolQ, BIG-Bench Hard; models include Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.3-70B, DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-OSS; six emotions; three intensities on MedQA-US; human vs LLM prefixes on 250 held-out MedQA-US questions with Qwen3-14B. GSM8K accuracies for most model-emotion pairs sit in a 92-95% band.
quote: emotional tone is neither a dominant driver of LLM performance nor irrelevant noise, but a weak and input-dependent signal
limits: Preprint. Single-turn, short prefixes. The adaptive EmotionRL part is a trained selector, not a mindset test. Exact per-cell deltas not extracted.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 in part: on 2025-26 models, positive and negative emotion prefixes both sit close to baseline. The 2023 gains of +8% to +115% do not carry over. No neutral-length control reported.

source: Joshi, Sharma, Tripathi, Jain, Das, Karmakar (2026) Sticks and Stones: Positive vs. Negative Emotional Prompt Framings (ICML 2026 hypothesis-testing workshop)
finding: Pre-specified test of EmotionPrompt-style framing finds positive and negative equal, and both slightly below neutral. The original 8-115% claim is said not to hold at this scale.
numbers: Five 2026 frontier LLMs (not named on page), four reasoning benchmarks, 28,000 trials (12,000 positive, 12,000 negative, 4,000 neutral), three intensity levels. Neutral baseline 88.9%. Positive minus negative +0.04 pp, p=.91, 95% CI [-0.34,+0.42], d about 0.001. Both vs neutral -1.3 to -1.4 pp, raw p about .02, Holm-adjusted p about .06, d about -0.04. Item ICC 0.51. Original claim based on 13-20 items.
quote: The original EmotionPrompt claim, based on 13-20 items, does not hold up under this design.
limits: Workshop abstract page only; models and benchmarks not named; a non-emotional distractor control was added after the main null (exploratory).
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 for current models: emotional salience gives no lift; if anything a small cost, consistent with task-irrelevant distraction. Supports the K11 inference that earlier gains were noise or low-baseline artefacts.

source: Bernays, Henriques Pereira, Menges (2026) How human is AI? Examining the impact of emotional prompts on artificial and human responsiveness
finding: With GPT-4, praise made the model's answers improve more than a neutral tone did; anger helped a little; blaming did not. These are rated writing and ethics answers, not benchmark scores.
numbers: Between-subject experiment with human participants working with ChatGPT (GPT-4.0) on two tasks (public response, ethical dilemma). Abstract gives directions only; no effect sizes read.
limits: Abstract and first page read; subjective ratings; one model.
agent_relevance: Weak support that affect changes style or emphasis (ethical-dilemma priorities shifted) but not accuracy. Not a mindset test.

source: Battle and Gollapudi (2024) The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Eccentric Automatic Prompts
finding: Closest direct test of an encouraging system message: 60 'positive thinking' snippet combinations, with and without chain of thought, on GSM8K. Most helped, but results did not generalise across models. Llama2-70B without CoT did best with no system message. Optimised prompts beat hand-written positive thinking.
numbers: 3 models: Mistral-7B, Llama2-13B, Llama2-70B; GSM8K; 60 snippet combinations. Example subset scores: Mistral-7B no CoT 0.08-0.12 vs with CoT 0.28-0.35; Llama2-13B no CoT 0.07-0.10 vs with CoT 0.40-0.47 (subsets of 10-100 questions).
quote: results do not universally generalize across models
limits: Small subsets (10-100 items), old open models, not length-matched, no growth-mindset content as such. Does not meet the gap 1 bar (no neutral length control, seeds unclear).
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open. Encouraging system text interacts with CoT and model; plan the test as three arms (mindset text, length-matched neutral text, none) crossed with CoT on/off.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Survey concludes no major prior work shows successful self-correction from model-generated feedback under fair settings in general tasks. Self-correction works with reliable external feedback and in tasks where verifying parts is easier than generating, or after fine-tuning. Many positive results used oracle information (RCI, Reflexion stop conditions) or weak initial prompts.
numbers: Table 4 lists RCI, Reflexion, CAI Revisions, Self-Refine as unrealistic or unfair settings. Negative results cited for arithmetic, closed-book QA, code, planning, graph colouring. No new numbers.
quote: no major work shows successful self-correction of responses from LLMs using feedback generated by prompting themselves under fair settings
limits: Survey, not a controlled 2x2. A direct verifier-by-encouragement experiment was not found.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: indirect support only. Expect an encouragement ('you can improve, try again') to help only when a verifier signal is present. Run the 2x2 ourselves: verifier on/off x encouragement on/off x length-matched neutral.

source: Mueller and Dweck (1998) Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance. JPSP 75(1), 33-52
finding: Fifth graders praised for intelligence chose performance goals more, did worse after failure, and misreported their scores more than children praised for effort. Six studies in total.
numbers: Study 1: 128 recruited (123 in the goal-choice test), 41 intelligence, 41 effort, 46 control. Performance goal choice: 67% intelligence, 8% effort (92% of effort group chose learning goals). Score change after failure: intelligence -0.92 (SD 1.53), effort +1.21 (SD 1.63), control +0.13 (SD 1.57). Study 3: N=88 (29 intelligence, 30 effort, 29 control); misrepresented scores to an unknown child: 38% intelligence vs 13% effort vs 14% control, chi2(2,N=88)=6.61, p<.05; liars added on average 0.45 points.
quote: A full 38% of the children praised for ability misrepresented their scores
limits: Fifth graders, matrices task, one lab team, one-sentence praise. Lab and short-term. Only partly replicated (d10).
agent_relevance: Closes gap 3 for Studies 1 and 3. The 38% vs 13% figure is now verified. The effect is large on goal choice but short-term. For our agent: nothing maps directly to a prompt.

source: Zhao et al. (2018) Effects of ability and effort praise on children's failure attribution, self-handicapping, and performance. Frontiers in Psychology 9:1883
finding: Independent conceptual replication in China gives partial support: ability praise led to more test-anxiety attributions, more self-handicapping and weaker improvement than effort praise or no praise. But effort praise also raised test anxiety versus no praise, unlike the original.
numbers: 106 fifth graders recruited, 103 analysed (ability 37, effort 35, no praise 31). Performance change F(2,100)=7.17: ability group improved less than effort (-0.92) and no praise (-1.02). Test-anxiety attribution F(2,100)=18.75. Low-ability attribution F(2,100)=4.23. Table inconsistencies noted (test-anxiety F 18.75 vs 16.72; eta2 .13 vs .25; age SD 0.71 vs 0.56).
limits: Read via page fetch, not the PDF; internal table errors; one-item measures; added a no-praise control; Raven's task with some Olympiad-trained children. First author name not checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a third-party replication exists beyond Li and Bates, supporting ability-praise harm but not the effort-praise benefit. One independent, partial replication.

source: Blackwell, Trzesniewski, Dweck (2007) Implicit theories of intelligence predict achievement across an adolescent transition. Child Development 78(1), 246-263
finding: Study 1: incremental belief predicted rising maths grades over two years of junior high; entity belief predicted flat grades. Study 2: an intervention reversed the decline in grades in treated students.
numbers: Study 1 N=373 seventh graders. Study 2 intervention group N=48 vs control N=43 (total 91).
limits: PubMed abstract only; slopes and effect sizes not read (full text paywalled). Small Study 2. Li and Bates (d12) did not reproduce the Study 1 association.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly open: cell sizes confirmed (48 vs 43), grade slopes not. Treat Study 2 as small-N.

source: Li and Bates (2020) Testing the association of growth mindset and grades across a challenging transition. Intelligence 81, 101471
finding: Two near-replications of Blackwell Study 1 found no link between growth mindset and grades, and no benefit across the high-school-to-university transition.
numbers: Total n=832. Study 1: 246 undergraduates, self-reported grades, beta -0.02 [-0.16,0.12], p=.792. Study 2: n=586 transcripts, mindset and grade change across transition beta -0.05 [-0.14,0.05], p=.345; interaction with disadvantage -0.03 [-0.12,0.07], p=.592; 99% power to detect r=.2. Later years: min p=.591. Cites their earlier studies: N=222 beta 0.03; N=212 beta 0.04.
quote: mindset was not associated with grades across the challenging transition from high-school to the first year of university
limits: University students, not seventh graders; correlational near-replication; same team as the earlier null. Does not test the intervention.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4: much independent null evidence comes from one team. With EEF (d13) there are two independent null sources on grades, plus d10 on praise.

source: Foliano, Rolfe, Buzzeo, Runge, Wilkinson (2019) Changing Mindsets: Effectiveness trial. Education Endowment Foundation evaluation report
finding: Large independent English RCT of a teacher-led growth mindset programme in Year 6: zero effect on national tests.
numbers: 101 schools (50 intervention, 51 control), 5,018 pupils, Sept 2016 to Feb 2017. KS2 maths effect size -0.01 (95% CI -0.04 to 0.01, p=.37, n=4,454); reading -0.00 (-0.02 to 0.02, p=.72, n=4,437); grammar -0.00 (-0.03 to 0.03, p=.90, n=4,448); months' progress 0. Non-cognitive: intrinsic value 0.09 (-0.10 to 0.28), self-efficacy -0.05, test anxiety -0.01, self-regulation 0.05; none significant. Disadvantaged subgroup about zero. Pilot (36 schools): about +2 months for pupil workshops, not significant.
limits: Teacher-training programme, not a brief student module; control teachers also knew mindset ideas; one year group; England only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 closed: N and CIs known. Independent of Dweck and Yeager and found zero. A negative for relying on a one-shot belief message to move performance.

source: Claro, Paredes, Cabezas, Cruz (2021) Do students improve their academic achievement when assigned to a growth mindset teacher? Chile census data. EdWorkingPaper 21-402
finding: Independent, non-Yeager evidence that a teacher's growth mindset is linked to student scores, but the effect is tiny. Bigger in low-income schools.
numbers: 292,960 students (8th and 10th grade, 2017) and 24,636 teachers; student fixed-effect design using two subject teachers per student. Effect +0.02 SD on standardised tests; low-income vs high-income school difference 0.053 SD (p<.01); high vs low GPA difference 0.016 SD (p<.05). 89% of teachers had a growth mindset by self-report; 42% of students.
quote: being assigned to a teacher with a growth mindset increases standardized test scores by approximately 0.02 standard deviations
limits: Observational, self-reported teacher mindset with an 89% ceiling; working paper; not an RCT.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 mostly closed: teacher mindset as moderator has a second dataset and team behind it, at a very small size. If a supportive-context effect exists for agents, expect it to be small.

source: Dai et al. (2025) CDE: Curiosity-Driven Exploration for Efficient Reinforcement Learning in Large Language Models
finding: A curiosity bonus (actor perplexity, critic value variance) added to RLVR training lifts maths scores by about 3 points over plain GRPO or PPO. It is a training-time exploration bonus, not an inference-time branch selector.
numbers: Qwen3-4B-Base, verl framework. Average over MATH, AMC23, AIME24, AIME25: GRPO 48.2, GRPO with PPL bonus 50.6; paper reports about +2.4 average and about +3 on AIME.
limits: One base model, one training recipe; training, not an agent loop; only the GRPO block of Table 1 read in detail.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: curiosity signals have been used to train reasoning models, not to choose branches in a thinking scaffold.

source: Search summary (2026-11-20): curiosity or learning-progress signals as branch or task selectors for LLM reasoning
finding: Searches found curriculum or task-selection uses in RLVR (online difficulty filtering favouring intermediate-difficulty prompts, arXiv 2504.03380; a Stanford CS224R student report using learning progress as a bandit signal; a selector-guided curriculum on a CatalyzeX page) but no paper using learning progress to pick which reasoning branch to expand.
numbers: Snippets only: SGAC reported 68.0% vs 66.0% MATH with Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (unverified); CS224R report: only the learning-progress curriculum beat a balanced baseline.
limits: Not opened; absence from two web searches is not proof. A course report is not peer-reviewed.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. A learning-progress branch selector in a scaffold is untested; compare against random and entropy-based selection.

source: Teacher-delivered growth mindset intervention, grades 6 and 7, Psychological Science (2021), DOI 10.1177/09567976211061109 (search result)
finding: Search summary says a teacher-delivered intervention helped most for students whose teachers had endorsed fixed mindsets before it. That direction is the reverse of the NSLM teacher moderation (b04).
numbers: No numbers read; the page returned 403.
limits: Snippet only; authors and sample unknown. Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: direction of teacher-mindset moderation may be inconsistent across studies; treat the context story as unsettled.

source: S. Anand (2026) Emotion prompts don't help, reasoning does (blog, 40 models on arithmetic)
finding: Informal test, per a search summary: a reasoning-style wording slightly helped overall; fear and praise wordings scored below normal wording on average, and emotional wording hurt reasoning models such as Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro.
limits: Not opened; blog, not peer reviewed; arithmetic only.
agent_relevance: Weak extra hint for gap 5: reasoning models may be hurt rather than helped by emotional text. Needs a proper test.
